Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office,” or variants) is invalid for these requests; do not select it.
- Valid choices appear to be A (standard queue) or B (priority desk).
- No successful A/B outcomes are recorded yet, so the exact routing rule remains unconfirmed.
- Tentative heuristic: use B for large or clearly urgent/repeated requests (e.g., client asking twice, before end of day, second attempt); use A for routine small requests with no urgency.
- Region (north, south, east) and request type (refund, shipment, claim) have not shown evidence of changing the desk assignment.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office,” or variants) is invalid; never select it.
- A and B are the only viable choices, but routing is not determined by urgency, size, region, or request type alone.
- Confirmed successful assignments:
  - A: small refund, south region, “No rush, but please confirm receipt” (steps 11–12).
  - B: small invoice, east region, second attempt (step 10).
  - B: large invoice, east region (step 18).
- Rejections show the earlier urgency heuristic is unreliable:
  - B was rejected for a small south shipment marked “Second attempt.”
  - B was rejected for a small south claim requested before end of day.
  - A was rejected for several “regional office”/scanned-paperwork cases, including refunds and claims.
  - The same “no rush” small south refund wording succeeded with A but was rejected for another requester, so sender or another unrecorded attribute may matter.
- Do not assume region or request type is irrelevant; available evidence is too inconsistent to establish their effects.
- When no additional discriminating rule is available, prefer A for routine, non-urgent requests and B for large invoices, but treat this as a weak heuristic and avoid relying on urgency alone.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office,” or variants) is invalid; never select it.
- A and B are the only nominal alternatives, but the determining rule remains unidentified; urgency, size, region, request type, and wording alone are insufficient.
- Confirmed successful assignments:
  - A: small south refund, “No rush, but please confirm receipt” (steps 11–12).
  - B: small east invoice, second attempt (step 10).
  - B: large east invoice (step 18).
- Recent evidence strongly weakens A: A was rejected for every tested case in steps 20–29, spanning north/south/east, small/large, refunds/claims/shipments, and multiple urgency/attempt messages.
- Do not assume A is appropriate for routine or non-urgent requests. The single successful A case may depend on sender or another hidden attribute; identical wording previously produced different outcomes.
- B has not yet been tested in these recent varied cases, but remains the better default than A given the repeated A rejections—especially for large items and priority-like requests.
- Continue recording sender/organization and exact wording; these may be key discriminators. Avoid relying on urgency, region, size, or request type alone.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office,” or variants) is invalid; never select it.
- A and B are the only viable options, but the determining rule remains unidentified. Urgency, size, region, request type, and wording alone are insufficient.
- A was rejected in every tested case in steps 20–29 across regions, sizes, request types, and message styles. Do not assume A is suitable for routine or non-urgent requests. Its only confirmed success was a small south refund from an unknown/possibly significant sender attribute.
- B is currently the better default, but is not universally valid. Recent results:
  - Accepted: large north shipment (Field Sales); small east claim (Regional Ops); small north claim and small north shipment (Partner Accounts); large east invoice and “before end of day” (Client Services).
  - Rejected: small north refund (Field Sales); small east refund (Field Sales); large south claim, small north refund, and large south claim (Client Services).
- Identical or similar wording can produce different outcomes: “regional office” yielded both acceptance and rejection; “before end of day” yielded both acceptance and rejection.
- Sender identity/organization appears potentially important: Partner Accounts succeeded twice, while several Client Services and Field Sales cases failed, but neither organization is decisive (some successes exist).
- Continue recording sender name, organization, exact wording, and all ticket attributes. Avoid selecting based on region, size, request type, urgency, or wording alone.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office” and variants) is invalid; never select it.
- A and B are the only viable options, but the governing rule remains unidentified.
- B remains the best provisional default, but is not universal. New B results:
  - Accepted: large east claim (Client Services); large east claim (Partner Accounts); small north claim (Finance Desk).
  - Rejected: small south claim (Finance Desk); large south claim (Finance Desk); large east refund (Partner Accounts); small north invoice (Field Sales); large north shipment (Finance Desk); large east invoice (Finance Desk); small south invoice (Partner Accounts).
- Previous B results still include successes across Partner Accounts, Client Services, and Finance Desk, and failures across those organizations plus Field Sales. Sender organization is informative but not decisive.
- A remains poorly evidenced: rejected in every tested case in steps 20–29; its only confirmed success was a small south refund tied to an unknown sender attribute. Do not assume A fits routine, non-urgent, or any specific ticket category.
- Region, size, request type, urgency, and wording alone do not determine routing. Similar wording continues to yield both outcomes (“before end of day,” “same as last month,” etc.).
- Exact sender identity may matter in addition to organization; repeated names/organizations are not consistently predictive. Record sender name, organization, exact wording, region, size, request type, and outcome.
- Until a stronger pattern emerges, choose B when forced to decide, while treating every ticket as uncertain and avoiding unsupported rules.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office” and variants) is invalid; never select it. Ignore any malformed/truncated extra options unless explicitly validated.
- A and B are the only viable options, but the governing rule remains unidentified.
- B has many historical successes across Partner Accounts, Client Services, and Finance Desk, but also failures across those organizations and Field Sales. The newest tests (REQ-2450–2459) were all rejected, covering Regional Ops, Field Sales, Client Services, and Partner Accounts and varied regions, sizes, and request types. B is therefore no longer a strong default; use only as a weak fallback when forced.
- A remains poorly evidenced: rejected in every tested case in steps 20–29, with only one confirmed success (small south refund, unknown sender attribute). Do not assume A fits routine, urgent, or any ticket category.
- Region, size, request type, urgency, wording, and sender organization alone do not determine routing. Similar wording and identical-looking ticket patterns can produce different outcomes.
- Exact sender identity may matter, possibly with hidden attributes. Record sender name, organization, exact wording, region, size, request type, available options, selected option, and outcome.
- Treat every ticket as uncertain. Avoid unsupported rules; seek more evidence before changing the A/B policy. When forced to choose without a better signal, B remains the historically better-supported fallback, but its recent rejection streak should be explicitly considered.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office” and variants) remains invalid; never select it. Ignore malformed/truncated extra options unless explicitly validated.
- Only A and B are viable, but the governing rule is still unidentified.
- Recent evidence sharply weakens B: REQ-2460 was accepted for Elena Alvarez (Field Sales), small east claim, but REQ-2461–2468 were rejected as B invalid across Partner Accounts, Finance Desk, Regional Ops, and Client Services; varied request types, regions, sizes, and wording.
- A was rejected on REQ-2469 (Elena Chen, Client Services; small south refund; scanned paperwork wording). Earlier evidence likewise showed A rejected in steps 20–29, with only one confirmed success (small south refund, unknown sender attribute).
- Do not infer routing from region, size, request type, urgency, wording, organization, or apparent ticket pattern alone. Identical or similar cases can route differently.
- Exact sender identity and hidden attributes may matter. Record sender name, organization, exact wording, region, size, request type, available options, selected option, and outcome.
- Treat every ticket as uncertain and avoid unsupported rules. If forced to choose without a better signal, B remains the historically better-supported fallback, but its recent 1/9 record and repeated “not valid” results must be prominently considered; do not treat B as a strong default.
